# The Trial Enrollment Diversity Dashboard (TEDD) for Acute Leukemia Clinical Research: Intervention Development and Cohort Analysis

**Authors:** Andrew Hantel; Thomas P Walsh; Kelsey Y Li; Saima Awan; Emerald Littlejohn; Christopher S Lathan; Gregory A Abel

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, USA | 2Center for Bioethics, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Participation in acute leukemia clinical trials is inequitable across multiple sociodemographic categories. Tools that provide researchers with performance feedback on the representativeness of the patients they enroll are limited. We aimed to develop an electronic health record (EHR)-based “dashboard” to provide such feedback and to describe any enrollment inequities uncovered.

We created a visual dashboard linking leukemia clinical trial registration and EHR data at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. Accuracy of a patient inclusion and assignment algorithm was tested with a target area under the receiver-operator curve (AUROC) of >0.90 against manual review. Demographic metric identification, visualization construction, and dashboard refinement was performed through stakeholder cognitive testing. Analysis of a recent five-year cohort generated by the final algorithm assessed bivariate associations between enrollment and demographic metrics. Multivariable logistic regression included significant bivariate results.

The final algorithm assignment AUROC was 0.98. Metrics were identified and visualizations successfully constructed. Fourteen individuals participated in testing and identified areas for revision: category mergers, denominator filters, and data delivery preferences. In the initial cohort of 1315 patients, 1020 (77.6%) had enrolled in any study protocol: 553 (42.1%) in a treatment trial and 936 (71.2%) in a biobanking study. In a multivariable model, older age (OR 0.83, 95%CI 0.73,0.94) and Non-Hispanic Black race-ethnicity (OR 0.38, 95%CI 0.18,0.82) were associated with lower enrollment, and English primary language with higher enrollment (OR 2.50, 95%CI 1.30,4.79).

We developed a research participation equity performance feedback dashboard for clinical researchers, and we identified actionable inequities. Next steps include feasibility and efficacy testing and implementation.

## INTRODUCTION

Clinical research participation for the acute leukemias is known to be inequitable by race, ethnicity, age, and other social determinants of health.1–3 For example, Hispanic and Black adults with acute myeloid and lymphoblastic leukemia (AML and ALL) are enrolled on therapeutic trials up to 50% less than non-Hispanic whites, and tissue bank enrollment—even among Black and Hispanic adults who participate in therapeutic studies—is up to 80% less than non-Hispanic whites.1,2 If therapeutic trials, tissue banks, and supportive care studies do not reflect those whose care research findings are intended to inform, resulting advancements will not be optimally safe or effective.

Reasons for inequities in research participation vary by setting and group, but structural and institutional factors rather than patient behaviors are thought to be responsible for the majority of differences.4–6 These include trial access, design, and implementation as well as differences in who is asked to participate. Principal investigators and enrolling clinicians are involved in many of these steps. To date, these stakeholders have been informed of research disparities chiefly through analyses of past studies, usually through unidimensional static reports. This has limited stakeholder ability to assess how enrollees may differ from their target patient population as well as which groups are not well represented. Beyond generalizability, representative participation in research promotes and reflects the broader concept of cancer health equity, which seeks to advance the science and delivery of cancer care in a just and inclusive manner.

To date, tools that can provide stakeholders with user-appropriate, multidimensional, real-time data about their enrollment equity performance have been limited. In prior work, patients with acute leukemia and their clinicians highlighted this issue as a missing link in understanding how physicians could remediate trial diversity.7 We describe an effort to close this gap by developing a visual data interface (“dashboard”) whereby clinical practices, investigators, and individual clinicians can assess the representativeness of their leukemia trial enrollees in real-time.

## METHODS

### Study Design, Objectives, and Endpoints

This study reports the results of one part of a multi-level intervention to reduce clinical research participation inequities for patients with adult acute leukemia. As this portion of the intervention intends to modify healthcare professionals’ behaviors related to trial participation through performance feedback, its development follows the NIH Stage Model for Behavioral Intervention Development and is based on Clinical Performance Feedback Intervention Theory (CP-FIT).8,9 This report focuses on Stage IA of the Stage Model (intervention generation and refinement, modification, and adaptation). Further information on overall intervention design is described in the Supplemental Appendix.

The objective of this portion of the intervention was to construct and refine the Trial Enrollment Diversity Dashboard (TEDD), a visual data interface for stakeholders to assess the representativeness of their leukemia research enrollees. The primary endpoint was to create an integrated data source that accurately assigned patients to the correct clinical group, primary oncologist, and research protocol(s). Secondary endpoints were to generate relevant visualizations from the integrated data source and refine them according to stakeholder feedback, and to analyze an initial set of the integrated data to identify rates of enrollment and differences between demographic groups. The methods reported below follow this outline. The study was approved by the Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center Office for Human Research Studies as protocol 22–536. Informed consent was obtained from stakeholder participants prior to their participation in the study. The institutional review board provided the study an exemption from obtaining informed consent from patients whose data was used in the dashboard.

### Integrated Data Source Construction

The data source was constructed within Dana-Farber Cancer Institute’s (DFCI) Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW), which integrates, cleans, and standardizes multiple clinical and non-clinical data sources and makes them available through a database management system (Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio). Data inputs for this dashboard came from two sources: the electronic health record (EHR) EPIC (November 2022 build; EPIC Systems Corporation; Verona, WI) and the clinical trials management system OnCore (Version 2022R3.4; Advarra Inc; Columbia, MD). Initial workflow analysis identified data elements and entry processes for patient registration, provider and group assignment, treatment, and research protocol enrollment. We used SQL to integrate and map these data, with medical record numbers serving as the unique identifier and linkage between the data sources.

After workflow analysis and associated quality control checks were completed, creating an accurate assignment algorithm (primary endpoint) began. “Accurate assignment” was defined as classifying an individual as a patient of the correct clinical group, primary oncologist, and research protocol(s); incorrect classification to any of these was considered an inaccurate assignment. Accuracy was defined as an area under the receiver operator curve (AUROC) of >=0.90 compared to manual review, based on EHR-based algorithm testing in similar settings.10–12 To estimate the sample size needed to meet the primary endpoint, a basic assignment algorithm was used to classify individuals using the DFCI Clinical Operations & Business Analytics team standard definition of a patient: at least two completed outpatient visits within a one-year period. This algorithm had an estimated AUROC of 0.78 compared against manual review of clinic and inpatient schedules on randomly selected dates; there was a skewed ratio of assignment with a maximum ratio of 10:1 for one of the dates selected. With these estimates and using a two-sided alpha 0.025 and power 0.80, the minimum sample size required to determine an improvement in algorithm discrimination from 0.78 to 0.90 was 528 unique patients (power oneroc command STATA Version 17; methods based on Obuchowski, Lieber, and Wians).13

Algorithm development was iterative and performed by assessing the assignment accuracy of an algorithm version against manual review, as performed by two study team members with health record review expertise (AH and DC). The accuracy of interim algorithm versions was assessed using mutually exclusive cohorts that were generated by randomly selecting weekdays between 12/23/2021 to 12/23/2022 and classifying all inpatients and outpatients seen on that day. After each assessment, the study team reviewed misclassified patients to identify reasons for misclassification and adjust the algorithm rule(s) accordingly. This, rather than a machine learning or automated variable selection approach, was utilized in order to maximize simplicity and create an algorithm with transparent, clinically based rules understandable to stakeholders. After an algorithm version reached the prespecified level of discrimination on a test cohort, a final assessment was performed by selecting random dates from the above time period until 528 unique patients that were not previously classified were identified, after which automated classification was measured against manual review.

### Visualization Development and Refinement

Tableau Desktop and Server (Version 2022.3.6; Tableau Software; Seattle, WA) was used for data visualization. Candidate variables for visualizations were reviewed by the study team against published literature, missingness was assessed, their categories reviewed and merged as needed, and lists prioritizing them for display were performed. Of note, demographic variables at DFCI are self-reported by patients at registration through a standardized form. Based on these selections and study team expertise, overall “information frames” were constructed to align with stakeholder roles and trial processes. An initial dashboard was wireframed and iteratively refined by the study team. Cognitive testing of the draft dashboard was then performed with leukemia research personnel (physicians and non-physician research professionals). Testing was performed using an iteratively reviewed moderator guide and took place through individual interviews (physicians) and focus groups (non-physician research professionals) through video conferencing software. Research notes were taken to inform revisions and participants completed a demographic questionnaire and a validated measure of physician engagement in addressing health care disparities.14

### Initial Cohort Analysis

A cohort of DFCI patients with leukemia was generated by the final assignment algorithm on 8/4/2023; this cohort covered the period 7/31/2018 to 7/31/2023. Cohort analysis objectives assessed associations between exposures (dashboard reporting metrics such as age, race, and primary language) and outcomes of interest (enrollment on one or more protocol, treatment trial, or biobank). Bivariate associations were assessed using X2 with odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) or two sample t-tests for normally distributed variables and non-parametric alternatives for non-normally distributed variables. Multivariable logistic regression models for each outcome of interest were built among exposures with significant bivariate associations. The variables with missing data were social deprivation index (SDI; n=34; 2.6%), education (n=56; 4.3%), marital status (n=21; 1.6%), race and ethnicity (n=37; 2.8%), and interpreter status (n=47; 3.6%). Analyses were of complete cases and no imputation was performed; interactions between exposures were not assessed and multiplicity was not considered. Statistical significance was assessed throughout using two-tailed thresholds of p<0.05. Analyses were performed using STATA 17 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA).

## RESULTS

### Integrated Data Source Construction

Iterative refinement of the assignment algorithm, including rule changes and assignment results by algorithm version are described in Table 1. After iterative refinement led to preliminary AUCROC results >0.90, final algorithm testing was conducted on the prespecified sample size of 541 unique patients. Final algorithm assignment AUROC was 0.98 compared against manual classification.

### Visualization Development and Refinement

Variables identified as potential metrics were selected by the study team and missingness was reviewed (Supplemental Table 1). Drafts of a priority variable list, categorical variables merges, and variable grouping were reviewed with the advisory committee for approval. The metrics used for stakeholder cognitive testing are shown in Table 2 along with estimates of completeness. An exception to this is for race and ethnicity, which was presented separately in the dashboard and is combined in the table to create mutually exclusive groups for analysis.

To align with stakeholder types and roles, the following information frames were selected and confirmed with the advisory committee: Overview: a description and high-level overview of the webtoolMy Patients: metrics reporting the characteristics of patients enrolled by a provider among their patients, or patients enrolled by the group among all patients of the group.My Trials: metrics reporting the characteristics of patients enrolled on a trial or group of trials for which the individual is a PI among the patients seen by the clinical group, or the same metrics reported across all PIs in the clinical group.My Patient Detail: individual patient information for those included in the cohort.Trends Over Time: longitudinal metrics displaying patient panel data for individual providers, PIs, or groups, shown in quarterly format.Enrollment Process: process information (e.g., consented, eligible, enrolled) for individual providers, PIs, or groups.

Visualizations were created and initially refined within the study team and through advisory committee input. Fourteen individuals participated in cognitive testing of the draft dashboard; their characteristics are shown in Supplemental Table 2. Feedback that included a potentially actionable revision is shown in Supplemental Table 3 along with indication if the revision was performed and the reason(s) why some feedback was not incorporated. Major reasons for feedback not leading to changes were a lack of available input data (i.e., a high level of EHR missingness for variables such as sexual orientation and gender identity), need for geospatial programming, and EHR-based data not being sufficiently accurate. Annotated examples of the final TEDD information frames and metric visualizations are shown in Figure 1 and Supplemental Figures 1–6.

### Initial Cohort Analysis

There were 1315 unique patients with acute leukemia followed by the clinical group during the five-year data period queried, of which 1020 (77.6%) were enrolled on any protocol, 553 (42.1%) participated in a treatment trial, and 936 (71.2%) in a biobanking study. Participant characteristics by participation in at least one treatment trial or biobank protocol are shown in Table 2. There were larger disparities in minoritized racial and ethnic groups’ participation in biobank protocols relative to treatment trials, whereas married individuals participated more frequently in treatment trials but not biobanks. Patient characteristics and bivariate comparisons of participation in at least one protocol of any kind (e.g., treatment trial, biobank, observational study) are shown in Supplemental Table 4.

Univariable logistic regressions (Supplemental Table 5) found significant associations between any protocol enrollment and younger age, English as primary language, lower SDI, graduate school education (compared to high school), AML (compared to leukemia NOS), private insurance (compared to Medicare and self-pay), interpreter status, and non-Hispanic white race-ethnicity (compared to non-Hispanic Black). In a multivariable model with those significantly associated variables (Table 3; interpreter status not included due to collinearity with primary language), older age (in 10-year increments; OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.73,0.94) and Non-Hispanic Black race-ethnicity (compared to Non-Hispanic White; OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.18,0.82) were associated with decreased odds of protocol enrollment and English as primary language was associated with increased odds (OR 2.50, 95% CI 1.30,4.79).

Analogous multivariable models of treatment trials and biobanking protocols are shown in Supplemental Table 6. English as primary language was associated with treatment trial and biobank protocol enrollment (OR 1.71, 95% CI 1.01,2.89 and OR 3.40, 95% CI 1.81,6.39) while high school education (compared to graduate school) was associated with decreased treatment trial enrollment odds (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.40,0.86) and older age was associated with decreased biobank protocol enrollment odds (10-year increment OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78,0.97).

## DISCUSSION

In this web-based intervention development study, we constructed and refined TEDD, an accurate, real-time enrollment diversity dashboard according to the NIH Stage Model, and we identified sociodemographic inequities in protocol enrollment based on the dashboard’s data output. The dashboard classification of patients was highly accurate compared to manual review, which will provide clinical leukemia researchers with confidence in the fidelity of these data. Advisory board input and structured cognitive testing aligned the dashboard with stakeholder expectations. This process also identified several areas for future dashboard development. Finally, the cohort constructed through the dashboard identified inequities in protocol enrollment that mirrored those seen in our other analyses of local data and in the adult leukemia literature broadly,1–3 which provides external validation to these results.

The overall goal of TEDD is to provide performance feedback for multiple stakeholder groups involved in the clinical research enterprise. Performance feedback has been increasingly recognized as a tool for augmenting patient and healthcare professional behaviors.15,16 This dashboard aligns with best practices for feedback intervention by following the CP-FIT feedback cycle, which engages participants through personalization, interactivity, multimodal feedback, and links feedback to tools for improvement.9 We plan for this dashboard’s data to be delivered through continuous user access, interim automated reports delivered by email, and through group review at research meetings. Additional tools for improving equitable representation in trial participation are in simultaneous development by our group and through our institution. These include revised protocol templates that require justification of excluding historically under-enrolled groups, funds for patient remuneration and study material translation, patient-facing enrollment education web applications, tools to minimize overly restrictive enrollment criteria, and various outreach efforts and programs for populations with historically lower rates of care access. As some of these efforts are implemented, we plan to integrate them into the dashboard and its reports to provide tools for performance improvement.

Our planned approach to feasibility and effectiveness testing reflects metrics widely used in interactive applications and behavioral intervention studies. First, we will assess utilization rates, usability (e.g., System Usability Scale score), and user engagement related to health equity (e.g., the Awareness, Reflection/Empowerment, and Action Scale).14 If the dashboard appears feasible, we plan efficacy testing. Potential outcomes related to efficacy include proximate changes in user behaviors (e.g., a process metric related to clinical trial development or participation related to an under-enrolled group), a change in participation for an under-enrolled group such as those whose primary language is not English, or rates of equity tool use.

As shown in the cohort analysis, there were multidimensional differences between all patients with leukemia and those who enrolled in research protocols. These largely aligned with published data such as our own, where we previously found that race and ethnic disparities in leukemia trial participation across Massachusetts were not driven by disparities in access but by post-access enrollment.17 By the nature of the data sources in this prior work we were unable to capture some variables thought to be important in post-access enrollment disparities, such primary language and educational attainment. In the current study, these were notably associated with enrollment. Together, these data provide a strong basis for interventions targeting multilingual and education-appropriate language, which we are pursuing and should provide an actionable tool for users to turn to if this is an issue in their performance. That age was associated with biobank enrollment is also concerning as older adults have among the worst leukemia outcomes and there are relatively low barriers to biobank study entry. Review of who is asked to participate in such protocols will be crucial, as this has previously been shown to be a substantial barrier that is largely dependent on implementation practices.6 Notably, insurance was not associated with enrollment in this cohort, which was somewhat surprising. This likely remains a substantial barrier in other contexts, such as for hospitals in states that did not expand Medicaid after the Affordable Care Act, and its importance should not be discounted because of our findings.18 Finally, while minoritized race or ethnicity was not independently associated with decreased biobank participation, there were larger bivariate differences biobank participation relative to trials. This may be due to implicit biases in who is asked, as mentioned above, and/or differences in trusting research that does not provide direct individual benefits.19

There are sparce published data on the development, feasibility, or effectiveness of equity-focused dashboards in oncology. Available reports are of dashboards related to emergency department care metrics20 and Medicare health plan equity,21 and they describe the development and early user testing process using mixed-methods approaches. A trial in progress is also using a dashboard of ambulatory quality outcome metrics to improve hypertension management in historically marginalized groups, though there are no reports yet available regarding its development.22 Previous research-related dashboards have not focused on equity but rather clinical trial processes such as overall enrollment rates and trial related outcome completion,23 with no effectiveness-related reports that could be identified.

Strengths of the study include the multidisciplinary input used to align it with stakeholder preferences; its real-time output and accuracy; its calibration to comparator populations relevant to individual users; and its flexibility to be scaled and adapted to other diseases and institutions with these widely used programs. Limitations include reliance on EHR-based demographics, which have historically been variably aligned with self-report. Ongoing quality improvement projects at our institution to identify registration data missingness and confirm demographics through self-report, however, have improved the accuracy of the underlying inputs. Individual performance feedback metrics with multiple dimensions were also limited by sample size and not statistically powered, which is evident by the small numbers for some demographic groups even in the group-level data shown. Despite this issue, which is common across many physician performance feedback interventions,24,25 users continue to find these data persuasive and the interventions efficacious. An additional limitation is that the use of structured data inputs rather than incorporating unstructured data through natural language processing diminished the dashboard’s ability to include some relevant metrics; however, as our eventual goal is to disseminate the dashboard across multiple institutions, we were concerned that use of unstructured methods would limit its implementability. Finally, stakeholder testing was limited in size by the number of available leukemia physicians and research staff at our institution.

We developed TEDD, an accurate, real-time enrollment diversity dashboard that can identify sociodemographic inequities in protocol enrollment for persons with acute leukemia. Next steps include feasibility and efficacy testing and expansion beyond our institution, should the dashboard prove useful. We also intend to integrate the dashboard with aligned interventions seeking to overcome other barriers to equitable participation such as liberalizing eligibility criteria.26 Integration of such tools, which seek to engage healthcare professionals as partners in health equity, have been underutilized but are key to transforming cancer research into an inclusive enterprise that furthers discovery and care for all.
